Recent figures from Denmark's Nationalbank show that companies using #AI are hiring 9-11% fewer people, epecially young workers and those with higher education. 

The figures should give rise to great concern. If start level jobs are being automated, how will young people ever gain the skills needed to learn, grow and progress in the labour market? What gaps are we creating as cohorts retire and experience disappears? What about the future financing of pensions, the welfare state? What about the economy? And not least how will this affect the young economically, socially and psychologically? 

Technology driven unemployment is not a new thing. But the widespread use of AI across all sectors will mean that employment will be affected across most occupations. The report from the Nationalbank states that 59% of Danish companies are already using AI. We can only expect that figure to rise. Whilst unemployment levels have not risen yet, can we expect them to? If so, then what for the young workers?

And what about the workers with higher education? Given that higher education is free in Denmark, we must ask whether the state is financing an unsustainable future? Who bears the responsibility? What will be the consequences of rising unemployment, a decline in buying power, less tax revenue and the resulting socio-economic changes? Technologies don't pay tax. Who then, will pay for the welfare state's continuation? And if the welfare state collapses, what then?

Many many questions and as of yet few concrete answers. We only need to look at countries with high youth unemployment to see how deep the crisis can go. China with 19% youth unemployment. South Africa 60%. 

Do we need a new social contract that obliges companies to hire new cohorts? How do we maintain quality jobs and decent working conditions if the competition for a job, any job, rises? 

What is the responsibility of older generations who have benefitted from economic growth and the universal welfare state towards the generations that follow? It no longer seems plausible that we can sit back and let the market  determine the future.

⚡ What happens when people can evolve their jobs faster than we can redesign them?
That has implications far beyond tool adoption:
→ Role definitions
→ Team composition
→ Career paths
→ Decision rights
→ Hiring profiles
#Expertise still matters. Probably more than ever.
But the future organization may be less about protecting functional boundaries — and more about #enabling people to move across them safely and effectively.

💡 The real opportunity may not be automating today’s job descriptions.
It may be expanding what people are able to do.
